utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I would like to apologise to the witness, to the parties and the public for the delayed start this morning and for the late change of the courtroom. Despite best endeavours of the Tribunal's staff, we were unable to commence proceedings in Courtroom III at the scheduled time due to a leak in the public gallery and the courtroom which caused a few ceiling panels to collapse. In the interests of giving the public access to today's proceedings, the Chamber has moved the hearing to Courtroom I and for the record, hereby expresses its sincere gratitude to the Mladic Trial Chamber for their kindness to accommodate our request on short notice. That said, would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, President Dodik. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic. I extend my regards to you, the Excellencies and everybody else present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please state your full name for the record, as well as your father's name and state your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Milorad Dodik, born on the 12th of March, 1959, at Banja Luka. My father's name is Bogoljub.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the translation, and I would also like to ask you to wait for the cursor to stop before you start speaking. For the record, please outline briefly your education.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I graduated from primary school at Aleksandrovac [phoen] where I was born. I graduated from secondary school at Banja Luka, and I obtained my bachelor's degree in political sciences in Belgrade. I'm a politologist by training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you do before you engaged in politics, or if you did anything?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Early on, as a young man I was politically active. I was president of the youth organisation in my birth place, that was at the time of former Yugoslavia. Later, upon graduating from the faculty of political science, I returned to the Laktasi municipality where I still live, and I was elected president of the Executive Board of the municipality. Since that time, I've been in politics. As far as my previous education and training goes, I have already described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a member of which political party did you run on the first multi-party elections and then were elected to your position at Laktasi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I became a member of the alliance of reformists in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was elected to the highest leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was president of the regional board of the Bosnian Krajina as it was known then. It comprised some 20 municipalities that gravitated to Banja Luka. At the first multi-party elections, I was a bearer of the elder role, and I was elected to the first multi-party assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before that war and after this war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Chamber who was the head of the political party at the level of Yugoslavia and at the level of Bosnia, and what was the party's position in terms of resolving the state crisis. The rest is perhaps not interesting.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The president of the party at the level of Yugoslavia was the then federal prime minister, Ante Markovic. And the republican organisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was led by Professor Nenad Kecmanovic. The basic approach to the resolution of the crisis was the preservation of Yugoslavia and that it should join the European integrations. The Prime Minister Markovic made great efforts to that effect at the time and many times, in conversation with him, especially after the war, and in particular over the last few years, he kept asserting that the leadership of Slovenia played the greatest role in breaking up Yugoslavia, and he could have prevented the breakup because the Slovenian leadership headed by Milan Kucan insisted on independence and secession of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as for democracy and economic issues, perhaps you could tell us just one sentence about the orientation of this political party.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It had at its heart free democracy and multi-party system, and free market was the hallmark of its attitude towards economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber how big was the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly in which your party won a certain number of votes, or rather, seats and what was the composition of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The composition was multi-party. This party that I was in won around 10 per cent of the votes at the time. There were a number of parties, the most important being the Party of Democratic Action, which was led by Izetbegovic; the Croatian Democratic Union, which often changed its president but I think that at the moment it was Mr. Kljujic; the SDS, whose president were you; then we had SDP which was led by Nijaz Durakovic; the reformists led by Nenad Kecmanovic; we also had the liberals and the Serbian Renewal Movement and some smaller parties. They all made up the political spectrum of the first multi-party assembly in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The first three parties I enlisted, the Party of Democratic Action, the HDZ and the SDS, began talks immediately after the elections and they constituted the authorities at the Bosnia-Herzegovina level while we remained in the opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your party defined as a national party, that is to say an ethnic party or was it multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: In our party, the members were representatives of all peoples or all ethnicities that was clearly defined and we all knew who belonged to which ethnicity, but it could be conditionally called multi-ethnic because it had the representatives of all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber what was the founder and the president of the party at the level of Yugoslavia by ethnicity. I mean Ante Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Ante Markovic was a Croat by ethnicity and he also hailed from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he was personnel from the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. He was the cadre from Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please briefly describe for us how this first multi-party assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina looked, in terms of how it faced the problems that were arising? How did you view the functioning of the assembly in view of the challenges which arose at the time, rather outside of Bosnia than in Bosnia itself. I mean Slovenia and secessionism.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, it was obvious that first of all the Party of Democratic Action which was the first one to be established as a markedly ethnic and ethnically oriented party in Bosnia-Herzegovina was persistently trying to implode the sensitive balance in Bosnia-Herzegovina through its activities, and the balance was based on the fact that there were -- and there are three peoples living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think the Serbian error and the error of the SDS was that it was trying to defend the break-down of the balance in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was caused by the SDA led by Izetbegovic. Throughout this early period it was evident that the SDA insisted on taking over all the jurisdictions and to control all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the beginning, we believed that it was proof that the right that had been acknowledged even earlier by the communist system should be broken down and that the aim of Izetbegovic was to create a unified Bosnia, a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina. Such conduct on his part and the part of his party caused national or ethnic based regrouping even of the people who were in other political parties and in particular it drew distinct borders between the peoples or ethnicities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, primarily the Croats and the Serbs who opposed this and the Muslims at the time because it was only 1993 that they constituted themselves under the name Bosniaks. It is my conviction that Alija Izetbegovic, in this period, worked hard to promote his Islamic Declaration which had been written earlier on and which requested for introduction of a society that would be based on Sharia law and Islamic values in this territory. He had clearly stated that in his Islamic Declaration earlier on and he was brought to trial in the former Yugoslavia because of that. We were well aware of the text of this declaration and I could see on a daily basis how the political goals stated in Alija Izetbegovic's declaration were being worked out in practice. The declaration clearly said that wherever the Muslims established the authorities, they had to organise an Islamic state and that as long as they were a minority, they should stay calm, be integrated in the society, but once they became the majority they should strive towards this goal without any doubt. So even though the SDS elected me as a political representative of the Serbian people who was supported en masse at the elections I thought that this was a policy of dangerous intentions and that in this sense Izetbegovic lay the foundations for the conflict which followed and which was dramatic in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The conduct of other political parties, primarily the Croatian Democratic Union at the time, was directed towards giving support to the independence of the Republic of Croatia rather than supporting the Croats within Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was why the Croatian Democratic Union was integrated on the basis of the principles aimed at the break-down of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question was: How did you view the functioning of the assembly in view of the challenges which arose rather outside of Bosnia. Then the witness moved into a discussion about, among other things, the Islamic Declaration, not a word of which is mentioned in the 65 ter summary that was provided to us. I realise when evidence is being led viva voce it's not entirely controllable, but I think given time concerns and notice concerns, that the accused needs to be a little more careful about assisting the witness in addressing the questions asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I leave it to the accused. Could you lead the witness in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In transcript, on page 6, lines 22 and 23, it is not correctly recorded what the witness said because it turns out that he said that the [In English] SDS elected me as a political representative of the Serbian people [Interpretation] And the witness said that even though I was outside the SDS, which represented the Serbian people and had great support, I could still see and I was involved in the political life. More or less like this. But the substance was that it was not the SDS who elected someone, President Dodik had his own party and he entered the parliament with it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Correct. Mr. Tieger, I have sufficient time and I have come here to talk. I have been called to appear before this Court and please do not interrupt me because the context I'm talking about is very important to understand how the assembly operated. Because without being able to understand this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The point was to concentrate on answering the question. Mr. Karadzic will lead you, if necessary. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did the political parties you mentioned posit themselves in view of unilateral secessions or the Slovenian initiative to break down Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: My party was against breaking up Yugoslavia, the SDA. The party led by Mr. Izetbegovic wanted an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. It wanted Yugoslavia to break down. The HDZ also wanted a break-up of Yugoslavia and it supported Croatia's unilateral secession both in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly, whereas the SDA [as interpreted] opposed the break-up of Yugoslavia and was oriented towards seeking a compromise for a continuation of joint life in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position of the Croatian Democratic Union as regards the secession of Bosnia, and what was its position as regards its internal organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I would like to say that I'm convinced, and the facts point to that, all that happened later, that Izetbegovic's decision that Bosnia should secede was a unilateral secession act. He did not have the power in Bosnia-Herzegovina that would allow him to make such a decision. When Izetbegovic made the decisions that Bosnia should be declared an independent state he did not have any Serbian representatives in the institutions of the government or in the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, such authorities were not constitutional and were not representative. Therefore, the unilateral secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina was something that was very transparent and evident and it was the cause of the later conflict. As for the HDZ, it at first supported unilateral secession of the Republic of Croatia at the time. It is a fact that its president, the president of the Croatian Democratic Union, was also the president of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman, which shows that this organisation had an identical goal, even though it was based in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second goal which was concealed was an alliance with the Muslims, that was the goal of the HDZ, and it had to do with making decisions about the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but evidently that was not sincere because several months after that, a war broke out between the Muslims and the Croatian Democratic Union and this war between them lasted more than two and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can take a look at the transcript, page 8, previous page, line 23, I take it the "SDA" should read the "SDS."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. Exactly, the witness said that but it hasn't been recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the Croatian Democratic Union in view of the internal organisation of such an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what was the position of the Serbian Democratic Party and also the Serbian deputies from other parties as regards the internal make-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The Croatian Democratic Union promoted and set up the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna which in fact established power in its territory. Their main political goal was the dissolution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and joining the Republic of Croatia which caused armed conflicts between the Muslims and the Croats, as I said earlier. So in the early stage of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, they used the opportunity of the organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina to support the secession of Croatia in the first place, and then later on they organised and implemented the plan to set up the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna so that it could secede the join the Republic of Croatia. As for the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS at the time, it should be said first of all that the SDS formulated policies which aimed at honouring and observing the political and constitutional system as was extant at the time, and it proposed that it should be expanded in order to recognise and observe the ethnic and people's rights in Bosnia-Herzegovina as the conditions had changed. In this early period of the multi-party system in Bosnia-Herzegovina, an initiative to form another Chamber which would be called the Chamber of peoples in the assembly is well known and the role of this Chamber would have been to protect the interests of the three peoples. The leading Muslim political parties and the leading Croatian political parties did not accept this, so the initiative of the Serbian Democratic Party which was launched and which we all supported did not result in any constitutional changes at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of majority was envisaged for the adoption of constitutional changes or amendments and the change of the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia and the internal constitutional issues in Bosnia-Herzegovina? What majority was needed according to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: A two-thirds majority was envisaged and it also included the involvement of legitimate representatives of all peoples and ethnic communities. That was why Izetbegovic himself could not tackle the changing of the constitution because he could not ensure that he would have the necessary majority and he wanted to redefine the constitution as the constitution of a unitary country. Whatever happened later was decided by the violation of this basic principle which meant that first of all everyone had to be involved, that the constitutional provision of a two-thirds majority had to be observed and that what had to be taken into account in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the carefully balanced structure that I will talk -- be talking about a lot today because it is the only basis on which Bosnia-Herzegovina can survive, even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now that you have mentioned today's Bosnia, can you say what are the main problems today as opposed to the period between 1990 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, it's 20 years later, but the political positions of course are almost identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, let me indicate to the witness it's my responsibility to monitor whether the examination is proceeding along relevant lines. I don't mean to interrupt him at all. So in this case, I wonder about the relevance of this question to the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I agree, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, bear that in mind. The situation today --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond to this? Your Excellencies, through this witness who is well-versed and is performing an important function now, I want to see whether the problems between 1990 and 1992 were caused by the appearance of one party or are they part of the nature of our relations in that part of the world? I consider this to be very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The situation today has nothing to do with your case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please try to remember how many deputies were there in the then assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and how many Serb deputies were there in comparison with the two-thirds majority criterion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: This is generally known fact, I suppose. I cannot remember the exact figure right now but I know that there were around 86 or 7 Serbian deputies from all political parties, of which the greatest number was of course from the SDS and then from the alliance of the reform forces which was my party. From the SPO I think there were two deputies and 83 deputies from various political parties. Due to the developments in November 1991, an assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established in order to show quite clearly the political goals that had to do with the way Bosnia-Herzegovina would be organised once it left Yugoslavia. I also participated in the work of this assembly and also other colleagues from my political party. There were representatives of other political parties as well, and they were not only SDS deputies, which indicates that we all understood the situation at the time and that we rallied around protecting the basic political goals of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of the particular political party to which they belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The indictment against me states that the time, or rather, the period when I joined the so-called joint criminal enterprise was October 1991 up until the 13th of November -- 30th of November, 1995. Can you remember whether the assembly was formed in October or in November? I mean the assembly of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Possibly it was October. I cannot say exactly now. There is information about that. It was in the autumn. But what is important is that basically this was a multi-party political assembly, not a mono-party political assembly. As a participant, I did not notice, and it wasn't possible to ascertain that later either, that what they say you are responsible for actually happened. The assembly of the Serb people wanted the Serb people to be protected and organised in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that they remain within Bosnia-Herzegovina with clearly defined rights as they should have, and that was legitimate and legal. No actions were referred to at the time, especially not violent ones, in order to ensure these rights. Discussions and agreements were called for, and that is what was pursued with the relevant political factors in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in that respect the indictment says that from October at the latest Karadzic took part in joint criminal enterprise and that the population of Muslim and Croat ethnicity should be removed on a durable basis from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then various crimes were committed, and the indictment lists them. Let us leave aside the fact that claiming right to certain territory is not a crime. Did you notice, ever, such positions in the SDS as described, especially with regard to the lasting removal -- permanent removal of Croats and Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I heard about that only later after the war, when indictments were being prepared for responsible people. I never heard at a single assembly or at a single meeting about the promotion of such objectives and you never said that. I never heard you say that, that you asked for something like that, and you were not in the function of issuing orders for anything, let alone anything criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago that after October, discussions were held and agreements sought. Could you tell the Trial Chamber how the negotiations process evolved. Until the end of March 1992, what kind of attempts were made to find a peaceful solution, from October up until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The very fact that after October and after the assembly of the Serb people was established, the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina continued to function shows that this was not a unilateral act. Rather, this was an act that was supposed to affirm the rights that should have been equal to those enjoyed by the other two peoples. There was also an assembly held in January. I participated in that assembly as well. And then a possible solution was discussed and also the establishment of Bosnia on a new foundation. So the Serb side and my party had certain proposals to the effect that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organised as a community that would affirm collective and joint rights of all. Of course, this could not come to fruition because Izetbegovic's idea was that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be a unitary country with a political system of one man-one vote which would mean that Bosniaks would have absolute domination. This could not have been accepted then and it can never be accepted in that area. There were many talks that were held and the most important ones were those within the initiative of the European union led by a Portuguese diplomat, Cutileiro, that resulted in the so-called Lisbon Agreement. That was well known then and that meant that within the Cutileiro Plan Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organised -- actually, you heard Cutileiro here, and I hope that you are aware that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be organised on a new basis. However, when Izetbegovic returned to Sarajevo he withdrew his signature, rejected that plan, and then continued his unilateral policy which shows that he did not want a solution, a political solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a participant, an active participant and founder of the assembly of Serb people and later on the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, did you take part in the process of accepting this Lisbon Agreement, this Lisbon plan? Did I report to the assembly? And also the acceptance of that plan in that assembly, was it sincere and resolute?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember that. I remember that meeting of ours. I just wish to remind you that you met with a great deal of resistance in your own party, but with your own authority you asked for this plan to be accepted. After that, the assembly as a whole accepted it. However, I must say that from that moment onwards, there were major doubts as to whether the other side would go for it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before that, the Serb community, and this assembly as a whole, did they make any concessions in respect of their best objectives and their first original interests and their best interests and did they accept that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be independent and on what condition?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: You said then that this was an unavoidable compromise and that it required giving up on certain objectives, and it was obvious through the debate amongst us, the MPs, this plan was not a full affirmation of all the previously set objectives. It was a compromise. You agreed to it and after that the assembly agreed to it, too, in order to preserve dialogue and the political process which made it possible to find a solution by political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how our acceptance to leave Yugoslavia on the basis of the Lisbon Agreement, how the Serb people as a whole took that and how the assembly took that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course, the Serb people took that with disbelief, primarily they wished to remain within Yugoslavia and they believed in that. We, the political representatives of that people, believed in the idea of Yugoslavia and that proved to be the best idea for the Balkan region. It is precisely the disintegration of Yugoslavia that led to major destruction in the Balkans and in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. The Serb people, that is to say accepted this with certain feeling of disquiet, but they trusted the leadership and they were absolutely prepared to carry out these agreements on the condition of course that peace be preserved primarily in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would the people have accepted to give up on that condition, too, that is to say the existence of our own entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Would the people have accepted a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, and which are the peoples that would have accepted a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Then, in the past and today, the Serb people reject a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that at the time you, as president, insisted -- I mean had you insisted on that concept then you would not have enjoyed any support because the Serb people needed a guarantee for their status. The Serb people live -- were a relative majority in the former Yugoslavia and they were supposed to be turned into a marginal minority in a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina and they would have been outvoted all the time and this was part of the awareness of each and every individual and that is why the political solution sought by the Serb people were such. You could not have gone any lower than what was accepted in Lisbon. The Serb people would not have gone for that. The HDZ at first pretended, trying to represent themselves as a party that wanted some kind of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, there was a clear objective that the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna secede from Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other hand, the parties of the Bosnian Muslims exclusively existed on a unitary system in Bosnia with a clear organisation, with a central republican power and the municipalities, without any kind of middle level that would have ensured equal national rights in the area. Definitely today I can say that one of Izetbegovic's major mistakes was that he did not take into account the sincere wishes of the other peoples who were supposed to be feeling free in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so his behaviour only led to increased fear in the other two ethnic communities, especially the Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak slower. The pace is too fast for interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could I remind both of you to speak slowly and put a pause between the questions and answers, for the benefit of the interpreters and us. Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the time, and probably today as well, these two communities, did they actually represent the Christian majority there and how is it possible to harbour that kind of ambition to impose a unitary concept upon this Christian majority by the Muslim minority?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I will not object to that question, although I think it appears initially to call for speculation, maybe the witness and the accused have discussed where they want to go so that it will be a response that bears on the issues here but I may be objecting to that depending on where it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the phrase "probably today as well" was unnecessary. We'll see how it evolves. Or could you reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm going to leave out the "today."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time these two ethnic communities, did they comprise the Christian majority, and how is it possible to expect that a unitary Bosnia be imposed upon them by the Muslim minority? I beg your pardon. And you established that they did not have two-thirds, but from this point of view could they impose their concept upon the Christian majority?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: According to the census from 1991, which was never formally adopted because it involved a great deal of wrong-doing, but at the time, the Muslims had about 46 per cent of the population, the Serbs 33 per cent, and the Croats 17 per cent. This was preliminary. And perhaps it is close to the actual state of affairs which shows that indeed in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Christians were a majority. Izetbegovic was, I have to go back to that again, it's a fact, his Islamic Declaration says so clearly, their political struggle for an Islamic state has to be one of perseverance. He didn't want to miss the opportunity of promoting those objectives then either. No matter what this looks like to anyone, you in the Chamber, you in the Prosecution and the public, I did recognise his activities at the time and how he was carrying out his political plan in an operative sense. It has elements of fanaticism, too. Probably there was also a concealed support that we could not see or recognise then, support that he received from elsewhere. That is why he persevered in his efforts, although they were not realistic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, this persistence in working for these objectives that were against the majority, how did this affect the outbreak of the war and the war option as such? What they wanted to achieve, could that have been achieved through voting and who needed war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and for which objectives?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Izetbegovic did not have a political majority; his political party didn't, his partners didn't. Without a majority that is needed for decisions that were -- involve representatives of the Serbs and Croats -- I mean, he simply did not have that kind of majority, and that is what the core of the matter is as far as the outbreak of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned. Izetbegovic then started falsely identifying himself as the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as he tried to rally international support for his project. Of course, this encouraged members of his ethnic community, and it persuaded them that they were right in their political objectives, as they tried to implement that political project. What is well known is that within Izetbegovic's political party, the so-called Patriotic League was established and it started arming the Muslims. This is best attested to by the fact that the first killings in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina were committed on ethnic grounds, motivated by ethnic principles, and it was Serbs who were killed by Bosniaks. The others, especially the Serbs, perceived this as something that led to affirming the necessity of better organisation in pursuing their national interests and objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you start over again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the Cutileiro Plan or the Lisbon Agreement. You said that the assembly heavy-heartedly but honestly accepted that plan, I mean the Serbian assembly. Did that plan make possible any use of force or eviction of Muslims and Croats from the territories that were to become part of the Serbian entity?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Absolutely not. There is nothing like that in that plan. It was very difficult for us members of parliament to accept that was because the autonomy under the Cutileiro Plan was such that the territory was not solid, and that gave rise to doubt among us members of parliament. But there is no mention of ethnic cleansing, the eviction of other ethnicities. We certainly wouldn't have opted for that kind of political autonomy of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As a protagonist of politics at the time, I refuse any such argument, and consider such allegations to be malicious insinuations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I -- I'm not sure that your words were correctly interpreted. It says solid territory. Did you say that the Serbian entity was to be made up of a territories that were not connected?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. That was a feature of that plan and that made Serbian MPs uneasy. The Serb autonomy was to be preserved but, still, we accepted that as -- in our will to preserve the peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The need for continuity, did it impose itself after the war broke out, and what were the six strategic goals in your understanding, the second of which was, I think, a continuous territory? And why was it important as the war broke out, whereas before the war we accepted discontinuity?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Before the war we accepted it because it meant freedom of movement and communication between the individual parts. Once the war broke out, many areas where the Serbs were the majority, such as mine, were isolated and surrounded. It was logical to strive to achieve continuity because only thus can you make possible political, economic, and of course military life at that time. I believe that to be a legitimate political goal because it was adapted to the new times. At the time, the Banja Luka region was surrounded and totally isolated. We couldn't communicate with other areas, economically, and for months we were unable to come by oil and it wasn't possible to distribute electric energy. We were without electricity for months. But if we made a mistake, well, I hasten to add that even today I would whole-heartedly vote for the decision we took then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about your party, you said that you were party chief at the regional level. This area was a centre of about 20 municipalities. From which time did associations of municipalities exist and could the individual municipalities choose to belong to one or the other?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Even before the Second World War, that area was organised administer -- administratively into banovinas. In socialist Yugoslavia, where there were six republics and two autonomous provinces all the republics had certain powers. In Bosnia-Herzegovina there were a number of associations of municipalities. They were free associations and their existence was conditioned by the interests of the municipalities at the time. The most obvious feature of their existence were the Chambers of commerce that existed at that level and the municipalities could freely choose to which association they wanted to belong. So it was up to the decision of the local administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A short while ago you said that the Lisbon Agreement did not envisage or allow violence or violent changes to the ethnic make-up. Do you know any municipalities in the RS, starting from your own, where the Muslim people did not, to a significant extent, leave their homes until the end of the war, and what did that depend upon?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: War certainly is not a normal state of affairs. War is characterised by a lot of violence and chaos, and it's very difficult to control chaos. It was important to prevent chaos but once it came about, those in positions of responsibility had to try to contain it. Unfortunately, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were many local warlords who tried to interpret the situation in their way and find their own responses to it. And such -- it was the same on all sides. As for your question, in my municipality, there has been a small Muslim community, and nobody bothered them. They didn't have any problems, especially not at the beginning of the war. When their crucial problem was the issue of weapons, whether those communities were armed and ready to enter into conflict with the Serbian people. However, that was not the case, the Muslim settlements were not bothered. And in Srbac municipality, there is a small Muslim community in the village of Kobas where the Muslims stayed throughout the war, and even today the majority of the population there is Bosniak. It's the same with the municipalities of Gradiska, Laktasi, Banja Luka. Where I live, things went the same way, and I was certainly part of political life. I was a member of the War Presidency of the Laktasi municipality, and I can confirm here that the Presidency never got instructions from the republican authorities to harass other ethnic communities in our area. I was an MP then, and member of the Presidency, and I had contact with the Muslim community. I can speak about some individuals from the time. I even gave shelter to some of them in my own house, because they were scared. And I think this shows that efforts were made to preserve peace and stability for all. Not all Serbs interpreted that properly but I never had problems, political problems, due to the fact that I had contacts and provided assistance to members of other ethnicities, that is Muslims and Croats. Where I live, everybody is familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. For the parties, transcript page 23, line 6 and 7, Mr. Dodik, you said that "even before the Second World War, this area was organised administratively into banovinas." I don't follow what a "banovina" means. Could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The former Yugoslavia was organised based on an agreement that was reached at national level. Banovinas are administrative units established by the then-authorities of Yugoslavia. Banja Luka was the capital of the Vrbas banovina. So even then Banja Luka was a regional centre, to which a number of municipalities gravitated. There were other banovinas in former Yugoslavia, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, due to the belated start of today, we are sort of pressed with time, tight with time. So can I ask you how much longer do you need for your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could speak for hours with this valuable witness, but I hope that I'll need half an hour to ask him all the most important questions, and possibly I'll need some more time depending on what will happen in the cross-examination. So my answer is about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is minded to take a break for 20 minutes at 11.20 so I would like you to conclude by then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, did you -- or, rather, were you criticised by the central bodies, that is the Presidency and so on, the government, for founding your political association at Laktasi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No. Never. There were some reactions by ordinary people who weren't politically active but I never -- I was never criticised by political institutions officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you gave shelter to some people. Can you tell the Chamber why those people were afraid? Did they fear the authorities or somebody else? I mean the Muslims in the Serbian areas.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: They were afraid of chaos, and instability. But it was the same for everybody irrespective of their ethnic affiliation. The very fact that you don't have electricity for years and have to live in darkness creates very strange circumstances and good preconditions for paranoia and fear, and if you add to that combat activity then that really is understandable. Let me mention a concrete incident. A Bosniak family and a Croatian family lived at Gradiska until 1994, when a sabotage unit from Croatia entered the area around Gradiska and the defence lines of the Serbian army and among the Serbian population they committed some crimes. That's when the Bosniaks and Croats became afraid, because some 14 Serbs had been killed in that raid. They were afraid from chaotic retaliation or something of that kind. Then I sat in my own private car and drove these families to Laktasi, which is some 30 kilometres or so away, and gave them shelter in my house. They are still alive today and can testify. I can give you their names but I don't think it's relevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Defence won't ask you about their names. If necessary, you can say them in closed session. How far is Laktasi from the confrontation line and where did your soldiers fight? Did anyone get killed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: In our municipality, in the immediate vicinity of Laktasi, there is the Banja Luka airstrip. It's three and a half kilometres away or up to 1 kilometre as the crow flies. In the early days of the war, the Croatian artillery shelled the airstrip and there were a number of people injured and one was killed. I was a member of the police at the airstrip. It was in 1992 when it was shelled from Croatia. Laktasi is some 30 kilometres from the border with Croatia. Like everybody at the time, the people from my municipality too were members of the Serbian army and under the command of the Main Staff they were deployed according to the plans in force at the time. Units from our area mostly defended the corridor which for Laktasi was a matter of life and death economically and socially. And the Laktasi unit was deployed from Doboj to Modrica to preserve the corridor for the functioning of civilian services. Once, a Mujahedin unit composed of the holy warriors of Islam raided them and killed 16 young men from my municipality in a single day. I remember the day when those 16 members of our unit were collectively buried. I must say that when I learned that news, I was with you at Pale – I don’t know if you remember - and we spoke about some peace initiatives. When you heard the news - I certainly remember it very vividly – you said that it was very painful and people were killed in war, but that we must keep a cool head and that there should be no more casualties. Naturally, this was consistent with my own value judgement of such events. Of course, Laktasi was affected by combat activities, and the municipality of Laktasi took part in the struggle for their own economic and social life, in the framework of the operations I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did the return of the bodies of those killed affect the situation locally, and what did we say who was -- should not come to harm due to such incidents?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. As with anyone including the Bosniaks and the Croats and the Serbs of course, death is a dramatic moment in life, in particular if we are talking about the numbers as high as those I mentioned. I think that general sadness was visible among anyone, whether the people were related to those who had been killed or not. What is important and what I wish to say is that in the conversation between you and me and members of my deputies group, as we were with you at the time, you said that in Laktasi we should pay our respects to those who had been killed but that must not cause a reaction that would threaten the Bosnian Muslim community in Laktasi. That was what we believed and how I understood that at the time. And it was explicitly stated in such a way at the time. And that never happened indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the safety of your Muslims was preserved?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. They had no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain a bit to the Chamber what the political life was like in the assembly of Republika Srpska, whether people were allowed, and did they feel free to speak openly? Were there any consequences? What was it like from the point of view of freedom of speech and democracy in the assembly considering that you were a fierce opposition and opposed anything stupid that ever appeared?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think that those who made analyses, and I can confirm that in the assembly of Republika Srpska, from the very beginnings, the right to speak out was promoted and cherished, so whoever was a member of the assembly and even those who were not but were invited as guests by the local officials or some other communities or representatives of various social categories had the right and it was possible for them to speak before the assembly. I spoke often, and my views about how to organise life, especially economic life at the time, were the focus of my activities. In sum, no one had any problems because he or she spoke before the assembly. I want to stress that primarily there were no problems coming from you as the person who was heading Republika Srpska or the prime minister or anyone else. Sometimes we may have had problems at the local level with inarticulate individual who did not quite understand the times but it was not your responsibility. In any case, I had the feeling, and so did my friends, that the assembly was continuously in session, and it was not simple at all to travel at the time from Laktasi to assembly sessions. You had to travel towards Bijeljina along the corridor and then via Zvornik further on to Pale, if it was in Pale, and very often the assembly held its sessions in different places from Banja Luka, Novi Grad, Bileca, Zvornik and many other places where assembly met, in Prijedor as well, where the assembly sessions were held and where as a rule all the deputies attended. Democratic discussion was pronounced especially when we needed to adopt legal regulations. Your role in the assembly was to present the situation to everyone and the freedom of decision making was never threatened. You did not request that certain decisions be taken. It was up to the assessments of the MPs. The assembly sessions lasted for many hours. Sometimes they would end late at night, even before dawn. We always made decisions by compromise. Sometimes it was difficult to achieve those compromises, but that is only normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, the Prosecution sometimes extracts certain sentences which may sound extreme or quite sharp as they were stated by certain MPs at the time. Can you tell us what were the rights that the deputies had --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is an astonishingly leading effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could the deputies freely express even extremist views and did such extremist views or positions adopted in the documents that were produced by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite opposed views about certain issues which reflected the political life, but the resolution that was adopted was always balanced. There were some extreme requests by deputies. I remember that the assembly should state its mind about certain actions, and so on, but that was never done. And in this respect, none of the deputies never had -- I didn't, as perhaps someone who was the most representative member of this group which held a completely different political positions never had any problems except for what I just said, some local inarticulate individuals who believed that they had certain rights and therefore I was in some conflict with them, but this is not even relevant for what we are talking about now. In any case I am proud that I was a member of this assembly. I'm proud of its internal functioning and precisely of the possibility to express any kind of political views. In discussion with many of my colleagues, they expressed a same belief and conviction. I believe that the assembly took all the most important decisions, and what I could decide by analysing this period ever since there is not a single decision that was made by the assembly or by you as the president which was not in accordance with the decisions made by the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a document that was adopted among the documents of the assembly which allowed for the possibility, let alone which ordered that lawlessness should be sanctioned when dealing with anyone, and in particular with minorities? Would the deputies have allowed that, and could anything like have been adopted by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: In my archives, I have practically all the most important decisions made at the time. They are available to the Trial Chamber and the public at large. I believe - I'm convinced - that there is not a single decision there that could serve as a basis for crimes, expulsions or anything such. And I believe that the position towards the events is something that is visible through the decision-making process. No one ever stepped up and said, We mustn't make such a decision so that we will not leave such a trace. No one ever said anything like that. We freely made the decisions that were adopted, and of course you as the president expressed your views as well, but I can also confirm that what you advocated in the beginning in some of the sessions was not always accepted in the form as you requested it. It was very often changed during discussion, especially when we talk about the certain laws that were adopted at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on our system, is it the president's obligation to attend the assembly sessions all the time, as I did during the war, or does it depend on the specific occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Only when requested, the president attends the assembly, and then he has to take the oath. You attended all the assembly sessions, even those that I did not attend though those were few. I believe that that helped to ensure the stability of this institution, and the assembly was definitely, with all due respect to you as the president, the assembly was the most important organ at the time. I believe that it even considered some issues which were the jurisdiction of the government, and that it therefore extended the scope of its activities. But in any case, I definitely believe that the assembly was the most important organ during that period, and that it took all the most important decisions in the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the political parties, there were several of those. Did your party or did the SDS order its deputies how to vote and how to act in assembly, or were there no clubs or rather no obligations to one's party during the war? How did these 83 deputies behave in terms of freedom expression and acting in accordance with their own conscience?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It was known precisely who belonged to which political party. Among ourselves we knew that quite well. And we respected each other completely in that sense. Apart from what is mere political passion, there were no special discussions or conflicts among ourselves which can be seen in some other parliaments. There was nothing that could create animosity or hatred between us outside of the parliament hall. We were united. And on many occasions, you and the leadership of Republika Srpska, not just as assembly but as the deputies as a whole, you would inform us as the very delicate negotiations and talks that you had with various factors from the international community about various contacts and communication you had with various international forums and a variety of contacts you had with other relevant factors in the region. As a proof of the freedom, I might note that in 1994, deputies who were not SDS members, formed an independent deputies group, and formally we acted as an independent deputies group, of which I was the president at the time. I then discussed with you, and you supported such work in the situation, even though there were high officials in Republika Srpska who did not think that it was good at the time and tried to persuade us. But we did not feel any problems. We never faced any problems because we set up this group and organised ourselves in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Even though we were not formally in coalition, was any of your members appointed to the first government in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Mr. Kalinic was the president of the deputies club of the alliance of reformist forces, the party that I belonged to, before the war, in the assembly, and later on they became the minister of health in the government of Republika Srpska which testifies to the fact that there were even offers to some members of our party to be members of the government, ministers in the government. For private reasons they declined, but in any case, this example testifies to what that was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You preserved your Muslim community in Laktasi. Did you participate with some -- my representatives, people I authorised, in alleviating the circumstances for the Muslims in some other parts? Do you remember Mevludin Sejmenovic who was a deputy from the joint assembly, and what can you tell us about your involvement and my position to -- with regard to the Muslims in that part of the country, the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I apologise. I think that we had an assembly session of the Republika Srpska Assembly after St. George's day, sometime in May, and it was then that, together with deputy from your party, I contacted the gentleman you mentioned, a Bosniak or Muslim deputy, and he was a deputy of the SDA, Izetbegovic's political party, and he lived in a Banja Luka suburb or he was staying there with his relatives. I went over to his house and we had a discussion about that with him. He felt some fear about possible further developments. We asked him to join the work of the assembly of Republika Srpska as a Bosniak, which as I felt he had already accepted, but later on he declined. Our position was that you and the parliament speaker, Mr. Krajisnik, should be informed about that in Banja Luka, at the army centre, where the assembly sessions were held. So we sat down together, we talked about that, and you just said that he was welcome and that you had no objections that he should be involved in the work of the assembly. Of course, later on he did not accept this, but other representatives of the authorities in Republika Srpska reacted in a similar way. So unless I'm mistaken, that was around the 10th or the 12th May when the assembly session was held in Banja Luka, in 1992. So the war operations were still not intense and we communicated with these people. As for the Muslim community in the Laktasi municipality, I would like to say that at the very beginning, as I said, I was the head of the police unit at the Laktasi airstrip. In direct contact with us was a Bosniak populated village. There were many people I knew from earlier on, and I have to say that then, as the police commander at the airstrip, I learned that an unofficial group of armed men intended to enter this village and square accounts with the Bosniaks, so I brought my unit there and I prevented them from entering the village. I was supported by all the local representatives of the municipality. That was around mid-1992. All the representatives of the authorities of Laktasi municipality supported me in this, and practically all of them were members of your party, the SDS. They remained there for quite a long time, and at some point just before the war, some people from that community moved out to Sweden. Others stayed. At the moment some people have returned. And there was no violence in that particular area, and I prevented one such potential act.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Mirza Mujadzic who was also with you in the joint assembly said during his testimony here that where there were less than 50 per cent of them, we did not do anything to them. How --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How is that not going to be a leading question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quoting what Mujadzic said that where they were less than 50 per cent, that we never did anything to them. I'm asking the witness how this fits in with what he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in itself leading. Why don't you put your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, whether there would be any conflicts, what did that depend on, religious affiliation or something else, say between Serbs and Muslims in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: First of all, I am not retarded in order to need to have anything suggested to me, and it's not that something can have a momentary affect on me so that I could present my position. So speaking of Laktasi, that would confirm the fact that where they were not armed, where they did not support military activities of the Muslims, Muslims were not touched, and there were no elements of conflict or crimes against them. This was not only in Laktasi. It was also in Gradiska and elsewhere. You could go there and see that houses remained intact there from the period before the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I know Mirza personally. He was one of the more prominent activists of that party on the ground and he organised the rebellion in Kozarac, which later led to certain things that happened there, and crimes as well. At any rate this just confirms what I said earlier on about Alija Izetbegovic and his Islamic Declaration, and in it he says, Where we are a minority we should try to keep quiet but where we are a majority we should try to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because of your overlapping, the interpreters were not able to hear the last part of the witness's answer. Could you ask the witness to repeat what the interpreters missed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that they got everything: Where we are a minority we should try to keep quiet and where we are a majority we should try to establish our own authority. Our own way of life. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll finish quickly, Excellency, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the following: What was put to many witnesses was that the high representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina disqualified them from public life, from political life. Can you tell us what you know about that, what you know about the activity of the high representative in relation to certain officials and what the nature of that activity was, and what the role of the high representative is in that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The high representative of the international community was established on the basis of Annex 10 of the Dayton peace agreement signed by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Croatia, Republika Srpska, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and some imaginary Bosnia-Herzegovina that did not even exist, but the international factor at the time accepted that it be represented by Izetbegovic. He did not have the power to sign anything on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The high representative had the role to interpret the Dayton Agreement as a document of international law that was signed in Dayton, and as such, he had powers to take part in the civilian implementation of that agreement. The high representatives, or rather several of them, permanently, in the period since that office was established, violated that agreement. The best example of that is Mr. Holbrooke's assessment, what he wrote in his book about his activity in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he says there: I went to Bosnia with a mandate of breaking up the Dayton Agreement. I had 800 employees at my disposal from the office of the high representative, and 35 million marks, no, dollars, per month, to do that. Everybody helped me with that. My friend Chris Patten, the representative of the European union, who said that the EU was asking for everything I was asking for, and that is how I broke the resistance of the Serbs in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the effort to create a unified state, for which many people lost their lives in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that I have faithfully quoted him. This speaks the best of the intentions of the high representatives. The mandate of the high representative was supposed to be to implement Dayton, not to break it up. And also in this way the Vienna agreement was violated. The high representative unlawfully imposed many laws. He even intervened in constitutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in this way, he served the purpose of the first objective of Izetbegovic's, the creation of a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina. He invoked the Bonn powers that he gave himself. In the Bonn powers it says that the high representative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Our time is rather limited. The question was about disqualification of certain individuals from public life. Could you deal with that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have time, I have no limit from that point of view, but I think that this is a complex issue and that this kind of introduction that I've been trying to make should be made. I'm trying to say that the high representative massively violated the powers that he had. He intervened in the constitution, changed laws, replaced persons who had been elected, and he didn't have the right to do that. He invoked the Bonn powers but that was not right. The Bonn powers say that the high representative can make decisions from the domain of decision making of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the council of ministers, but not in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Throughout the civilised democratic world, it is the parliament that passes laws. It is only in Bosnia-Herzegovina that the high representative passed laws and dismissed people in this way. Hereby a certain practice was established that leads to problems that Bosnia faces to this day, the Venice commission also rejected this kind of conduct on the part of the high representative. But he declared himself to be beyond the law and above the law, and it is impossible to do anything about this. And this is a good opportunity for me to say that the high representative massively violated the Dayton Agreement to the detriment of the Serb people and the autonomy of Republika Srpska that we obtained on the basis of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just another brief question: During your career, were you commended? Did you receive any decorations? Did you receive any awards?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: From the very beginning, while I was still a student, and while I worked in the former Yugoslavia, I always got top honours. In the army of the former Yugoslavia, where I served, I was commended as the best soldier of that generation, and later on, the highest decorations of Republika Srpska were bestowed upon me. You decorated me, like all other members of the war parliament, and later on I also got top decorations for my work from the representatives of other countries. My political efforts have only been aimed at peace and stabilisation. That's the way it was, as you know full well yourself during the war too, and I must say that I was one of the persons who advocated the acceptance of certain international agreements, although they were not the very best for us. Now I'm glad that that was not accepted because we would not have had this degree of protection of our rights in that respect. I consider this to be quite normal in political activity, that with regard to different questions there are different attitudes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, at this point in time I have no further questions for President Dodik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for 20 minutes. But before that, Mr. Dodik, I was informed indirectly through the Registrar that you should leave around 3.00. Could you confirm that? Tell us how late you can stay at the Tribunal today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For as long as necessary. Well, before that was the tentative time, but since there is a government plane waiting for me, I can extend that time, no problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I appreciate it. We'll have a break for 20 minutes and resume at 10 to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dodik.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, first I wanted to simply put on the record what those of us in the courtroom were aware of, but the Trial Chamber would not have known and that is that with the permission of security, you had an opportunity before court began to greet and kiss Mr. Karadzic, that is before the Judges entered the first time. Mr. Dodik, today, as has been our practice, I have the opportunity to ask you certain questions about your evidence, and I expect to focus on very particular issues and the Judges encourage us to cover them as efficiently as possible. And in that connection, let me advise you that we have the benefit of both your previous testimony in the Brdjanin case, and a previous recorded interview you gave to the OTP in 2003 that you also confirmed during the course of the Brdjanin case. So it's my intention to focus, if not exclusively, for the most part on information you've provided before in the hopes of maximising the efficiency -- the efficient use of the time we have. Now I mention that in part because I am -- by simply citing you or referring you to something you said before, that doesn't mean I'm asking you to repeat it or further elaborate on it. I'm trying to focus on very specific issues. And although I don't wish to interrupt you, if we stray beyond the questions raised, I will do so in the interests of maximising the efficient use of our limited time. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I understand this. However, I reject any possibility of you quoting any of my previous statements. We have already discussed that when I testified in the Brdjanin case. I told you that I have not signed it, that I haven't authorised it, and if you continue to use documents of that kind I'm going to consider it a -- really something that I cannot accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, I tried to be very clear in telling you that I had -- I intended to use only information that you provided that had been recorded and transcribed, so that there is no question of your having concern that it wasn't something you said, okay? So that's what I wanted to let you know at the outset. My references will only be to such information. So let's begin.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: All right. I said, and of course I can confirm that we did have a conversation. However I've never signed this, I've never authorised it, and that is why I think you should focus your question on other things and not to refer to that particular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, for the third time I'm saying I don't have the intention of referring to that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Why don't you start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Dodik, let me ask you if you accept or deny or claim you don't have any information one way or another that massive crimes were committed by Bosnian Serb forces against Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats during the course of the war and as we will be discussing in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: We had a civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and military forces were organised of both the Bosnians and the Serbs and the Croats. All three sides violated the laws of war and committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Given your political background, let me ask you some questions about the political structures and authorities that were operative in the area of Republika Srpska generally and then -- and more specifically in the area where you resided. First of all, with respect to the SDS generally, which was discussed to some extent during your examination-in-chief today, that's -- you talked about the hierarchy and organisation of the SDS during the course of the Brdjanin case, and do you confirm that you said the following: First, that "this was a firmly organised political party with clear cut hierarchy and superiority"? That, "the SDS was a compact, well structured organisation in which the hierarchy was respected," and that "the party was internally highly homogenised and it functioned in a highly disciplined fashion"? And for benefit of the parties those references are found at transcript pages 20468, 20542 and 20469.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The SDS was formed in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the establishment of the Party of Democratic Action. It won the elections. It was one of the winners precisely because it was as you mentioned and as I earlier claimed that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Further, the party was controlled from the top, asked that question in Brdjanin, you said, "Yes, absolutely. Mr. Karadzic was president of the party which had its Main Board." That's at 20468. And you also said at 20474, "The top, leadership of SDS headed by Karadzic was at that time the uncontested leadership." Those are also correct propositions; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, I am also the uncontested president in my political party. Hierarchy is observed and this is normal for any political party, so I do not see what I need to confirm here. I said that I mentioned this about the pre-election campaigns when I was in one political party and he was in another, and so we fought as opponents of different political parties. They were well organised political party just like the SDA was and the HDZ and the Reformist Party and the party organs were respected and hierarchy was observed, then as it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, you also testified in the Brdjanin case that if the Main Board issued instructions the municipal boards and the regional boards were obliged to carry out those instructions. That's at 20468.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Once again, I do not understand why you're asking me a question about something that is included in the statute of that political party and in the statutes of all other political parties. Yes, it's quite logical that a political party, a political organisation, with a clear structure -- that the decisions of the highest organs are observed by the lower rank party structure. I don't see how the SDS is different in that from any other political party or structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you confirmed at page 25 -- 20514 in your Brdjanin testimony that you gave a tape recorded interview to the OTP in July of 2003, and I wanted to ask you about it in addition to some of the things you said there. Because during the course of that discussion, you explained some of the ways in which the SDS hierarchy was effected and among the things you said, when you were asked if you could provide a sense of the hierarchy and -- of the SDS and how it controlled the regions and then the local municipalities, you said: "Well, it's quite clear. They had their own people in the municipalities, that is the municipal board, presidents of the municipal boards and the leadership of these boards, and they were elected with the full approval of Karadzic and the leadership from Pale. Otherwise they couldn't have been elected." And that's found at --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Where can that be found?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It can be found at page 16 in English and B/C/S of 65 ter 24921. Do you need to see that, Mr. Dodik, or can you confirm it without a -- that that's an accurate assessment that you made at the time and that it is what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
