utterances.text: Well, I asked you not to use that report because it isn't authorised. I don't -- I cannot back it up and you're suggesting certain answers which you shouldn't do. I did have that conversation, but I did not authorise its authenticity. I think that you're trying to trap me here. As far as the SDS is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I advise you that it is for the Prosecution to put their material to you, but you're free to answer in the way you like to answer. You can say that it was true that you said so, or you can say -- you could say otherwise. Do you understand that, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand it quite well, sir. But I don't understand the intention, because a long time back, in 2003, and the Brdjanin case, the Prosecutor and I spoke about this topic and we said what I have repeated now, that he should not refer to this conversation, and he replied, Okay, fair enough. I'll try you -- I'll ask you the same question, it's a question with the same content, but without referring to this conversation or interview. The SDS certainly had a strong structure just like all political parties and I'm trying to think what could be so specific. Of course, nobody can become president of a municipal board without my approval. So, yeah, it must have been like that in the SDS, but the only contentious thing here is that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to try once more to clarify this for you, Mr. Dodik, so we don't have an unnecessary problem. First of all, I think the reference that you made to the lawyer saying it was okay to proceed in another way was to something Mr. Ackerman asked you, the Defence attorney. But more importantly, for this purpose, that was a reference to the interview over the course of four days that you did not sign, and that was what you asked not to be asked about, and that's what Mr. Ackerman agreed not to ask you about. But both -- but the taped interview that was conducted shortly before you testified in Brdjanin was indeed the subject of discussion. You confirmed it. Your words are on there. So that's a different matter. That's why I indicated to you today, knowing your sensitivity about the earlier statement which you did not sign, that I did not intend to ask you about that but only about matters that had been -- that you had -- where you had stated something and it had been recorded. Perhaps that assists.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I didn't even know that it was taped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you -- as I said, at page 20514, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why don't we look at the first page, 24921, right. And as we can see from the first page it provides the date of the interview and the persons present and it begins by saying, "Now, Mr. Dodik, are you aware this conversation is being tape recorded?" And you say, "Yes, I am." And you were asked, "And we have your permission?" And you say, "Yes, you do." That's the interview that I'm referring to in addition to your Brdjanin testimony.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I can discuss any topic but I see that you insist on this interview. But go ahead, whichever way you think fit. You could have written anything in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's all on tape, Mr. Dodik. You want to hear the very beginning to hear your own voice and to hear your agreement that it can be taped?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson? Just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would suggest Mr. Tieger just ask the witnesses the substance of what he wants to know. If it's inconsistent with something that's in that recording he can use it at that time, but we are expending a huge amount of time putting prior statement to a witness. It's only supposed to be put to a witness when there is an inconsistency or a need to refresh his recollection. So if Mr. Tieger can simply put the proposition of the question without reference to any statement or testimony if he doesn't get the answer that he wants he can then go and take that next step. I think we would all benefit from that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can assist in finding a solution. There are two interviews, and the witness must be told which one was tape recorded because the Prosecution interviewed President Dodik twice. I have one of these interviews before me, but this is not the one I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tieger was clear about that point but as to the way in which Prosecution put its proposition, it is Defence's position to ask for the references. I think what -- that's what Mr. Tieger was doing, but I'll leave it to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's try to proceed and maybe we had some unnecessary friction and we will have better luck in eliciting information as we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was also the case with respect to the SDS hierarchy that the SDS had their people posted in the media, in the police, and other structures; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: They were the party that was in power, and it was normal for them to do that. Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at one point, there were commissioners appointed to the municipalities who were people from the core leadership or connected to the core leadership, who had the power to give orders to the local authorities and the organs of authority; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I know that there were commissioners, but the way I understood it they were commissioners for the political party. I said earlier that I was a member of the War Presidency, but I was not in the position to get such orders from these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is true that you knew the commissioner for your area, that is Gradiska, Laktasi, and Srbac, and that person had the power to give orders to the local authorities and the organs of authority, isn't that right, because that's what you said at page 16 through 17 of P24921 [sic], the recorded interview.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Answering to the previous question, I explained how I saw these commissioners. Yes, I know who was there, and the SDS got almost 90 per cent of the votes. He worked with the party structure, and knew what the decisions of the executive power would be, but I can repeat that it's a normal thing even today in many countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to issues of discipline or control, it's correct, is it not, that SDS members who didn't agree with decisions were minimised or rendered passive, and that differing views were not tolerated in the period late 1991 to the fall of 1992, and that those references can be found in the Brdjanin testimony at 20470 and 20542.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Just for Mr. Tieger's benefit, it's not necessary to give us the references unless we ask for it. I think that would make things simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Can you answer the question, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. All that time, and even now, I'm a member of another political party. Speaking about another political party must be seen as a political discourse, and not everything that we say about our political opponents is trustworthy. The SDS was and still is a party with a clearly defined structure and party discipline must be abided by. I think it's normal that whoever dissents is marginalised or expelled from the party. It's the same thing in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Croatia. Wherever there are problems within a political party, the minority must either keep quiet or leave that party. That's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's also true that in the context of 1991 and then moving into 1992 with the conflict, that the use of the term "traitor" or the power of the term "traitor" was also present in terms of the exercise of party control; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That word was used even more widely in the whole society, and it was used by the Bosniaks, too, and the Croats, and so did we. I don't see what is less than normal there. Yes, I can confirm that, but I don't think it was anything special or abnormal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And one of the consequences of that approach was that those who didn't follow the SDS programme were considered traitors, and there were various ways of ensuring loyalty. For example, if you were not with them then the threat was that you could be immediately mobilised and thrown to the most dangerous part of the front, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases, of course. But it was not the rule. I know of some such cases. But it was more at a local level, possibly as the result of other things, too, not only obedience. But in such a chaotic situation as the war even, there was such cases too, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded that the witness said the result of animosity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, can I ask you again to speak more slowly. Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the record there is a reference earlier to P24921. It should be 65 ter 24921 so we don't have to make a later correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, let me ask you then about some of the reflections or expressions of these principles or approaches in the context of the area where you resided, that is in the Krajina region. First of all, as you testified to at some length in the Brdjanin case, the -- in the Krajina region there was the Autonomous Region of Krajina and as we will discuss the autonomous region of Krajina Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: There were Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the autonomous region of Krajina was a reflection of SDS efforts and interests; correct? It was something that the SDS, that had been present with the SDS for quite some time, even before its formal creation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, but I've already said that there was a war and a crisis going on, I said that the Krajina was completely isolated, that it had no communication, it did not have enough electricity or oil. It was very hard to keep life going, and of course these questions had to be resolved. The SDS was the leading political party in the area, but today and before I said to you that I was part of that structure in my municipality as a member of the National Assembly. I was duty-bound to take part in the work of these institutions. We dealt with questions that had to do with these economic and social aspects of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, but I want to focus on the autonomous region of Krajina for a moment, not the National Assembly. Let me ask the question a different way. The idea of creating certain autonomous regions was very present in the then-governing party that represented the Serbian people, and that was the SDS; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The regions existed earlier on and it was known exactly what Krajina, Semberija, Posavina, Herzegovina were, what the Neretva region was, and so on. So as an idea to establish a new social order, the idea of these regions did not exist as such, but the idea of establishing these regions with a view to the organisation of life, I believe that that was the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you -- and the -- it's the case that the decisions that were brought there, that is of the autonomous region of Krajina Crisis Staff or assembly, were basically discussed and agreed on before that in the SDS, and the SDS had indeed established a very strict party discipline in that regard? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. How can the witness know what happened in the party, in another party that was a political adversary? It is speculation that is being asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is to be assumed -- I mean, I'm speaking on the basis of the experience of my own party, political parties, if you will, speak -- function in a similar way before going -- before parliament. They have discussions and agree how they are going to position themselves in parliament. I think that that's what we do today and that's what we did before, and that's the way things have been ever since multi-party systems in the world came into being. So why would anyone suggest anything to the deputies club? Before every session of parliament, my political party has a session to see how they are going to position themselves regarding particular issues that are to be discussed. So I assume that that is the case with the SDS. So at these levels from the level of the municipality to the level of the autonomous region of Krajina, I cannot confirm that Mr. Karadzic was ever present and that he took part in the decision-making process of these organs. I don't know about that. Perhaps somebody else knows about that, but I do not know and I cannot say that he was in charge of these organs in that way. As for political parties, from the point of view of regional interest, members of parliament can behave any way they think that they should behave.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speaker please be asked to speak slower. It is too fast for interpretation for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, again asked by the interpreters to speak more slowly. Mr. Karadzic, I was about to overrule your objection but the witness has answered the question in any event. I take it Mr. Tieger was putting his -- this question based upon his -- Mr. Dodik's previous statement or testimony, so -- and Mr. Robinson didn't ask for the reference. So that was the reason why I was about to overrule your objection. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, you seem to be suggesting here, perhaps in response to what Mr. Karadzic said, that what you say about the Autonomous Region of Krajina, its hierarchy and input, was based on assumptions, but that's not what you said in the Brdjanin case when you testified at length about the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff, for example. So you said at page 20493, as far -- that -- that what you stated was, as far as I knew the situation in relationships there and that's what I inferred on the basis of many conversations with people who then and later confirmed such impressions. Or you said at page 20516 in response to questions from Mr. Ackerman, Mr. Brdjanin's attorney, so can we save a little bit of time he said so can I understand that when you say you have this opinion or impression it's based not only upon your observations at the time but on your conversations with people since that time, am I correct in that? In other words you're not just guessing it's based on something you observed and heard? Now, that's what you said in Brdjanin and you confirmed that that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I have a proposal. You have what I said in the Brdjanin case and that's okay. What's the difference between what I said in response to that question before and what you said just now? Of course, I communicated. I was not isolated and it's only logical that I talk to other people about these questions. From this position, I believe that that is quite normal, that a political party, before it makes decisions in the legislation and in government, that they see what their views are going to be and behave accordingly. I see no lack of consistency in that respect and with small modifications, basically the essence is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. You also mentioned in your earlier response something about whether or not Mr. Karadzic was present or took part in the decision-making process of the ARK Crisis Staff. Mr. Brdjanin was president of the ARK Crisis Staff, and Mr. Brdjanin could not have become president of the ARK Crisis Staff without the blessing and authorisation of Radovan Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: We can just make assumptions about that. I don't know what your information is. But I think that Brdjanin was chosen by the Crisis Staff. Whether there were interparty consultations, that is something I can just assume but I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, that is precisely what you said on the 17th of July, 2003, in the tape-recorded interview at page 6 of the -- excuse me, page 7 in e-court of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in front of us. Why don't we see the page? Is this part where the witness said, "I don't think so"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, those were your words at the time. Now, Mr. Dodik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you find the passage, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, and I'm not interested. I've already told you that I did not authorise this and I don't stand by this and you use it whichever way you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. It is a tape recorded interview as you saw before. This passage reads like this: "Could Brdjanin have become president of the ARK Crisis Staff without the blessing or authorisation of Radovan Karadzic?" And you answer: "I don't think so."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There you go. So what did I confirm?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that this translation is right. He said, "I don't believe so." He did not say, "I don't think so. "

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not make any assertions. If I said I don't think so, it's just an assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is for the Prosecution now to put their questions. So could you listen to the question and try to answer the question. Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As long as we are on the subject of assertions, you also went on to say, as I believe you did in Brdjanin as well, that you considered Dr. Vukic to be, from a practical point of view, a more important person on the ARK Crisis Staff than Mr. Brdjanin because Dr. Vukic was the president of the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: This is what it says here. I think it is him. That's what you should have said. I think that he is the president of the party then -- had a very important role in terms of certain matters, the most important one, that is what is written here. That is what I say, "I think." I'm not saying "I assert" or "I claim."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you went on to say, he - he meaning Dr. Vukic - had to have full support and absolute support of the approval of Karadzic because without it, he couldn't have been the president which also gave him power at the local level. That's what you said in July 2003; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That is written here, and in the context, yes, this would be correct, so I think that's the way it was but I could not know of all the internal relations of the SDS because I was not a member of the SDS, and I had information only based on contacts with people and that's why I said here very precisely that that's what I think. I did not make any assertions though. Now I think that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it was further your understanding at that time that in 1992, the municipal Crisis Staffs functioned jointly with the regional Crisis Staff and that the orders that the regional Crisis Staff gave to the local Crisis Staffs were respected; correct? And you can find that at the next few lines as well.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, the organisation we discussed a moment ago, to organise economic and social life, that seems quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Can you imagine what it would have been like had everybody done whatever they wanted? Of course, there was some co-ordination. I know of some certain economic matters where there were some joint decisions and that is not being contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, actually I wasn't asking you about your earlier testimony about the Association of Municipalities, but I was asking you about the ARK Crisis Staff and I was asking you specifically about your assertion in July of 2003 that the orders that the regional Crisis Staff gave to the local Crisis Staffs were respected. That's what you said then. That was the case; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I believe that it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you also discussed -- let me ask you this: It was also the case that you discussed in your -- you were aware of an article on the 27th of February which was brought to your attention, that is an article that was published on the 27th of February, 1992, that was brought to your attention during the course of the Brdjanin case involving issues between Mr. Krajisnik and Brdjanin in that latter part of February 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I came here as a witness in Mr. Karadzic's case. I was not preparing for either Brdjanin or Krajisnik. At any rate, well, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Maybe, but I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is about Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Dodik. And I only mention that to place it in temporal context for you, because it was around that time, wasn't it, that Mr. Karadzic came to Banja Luka to discipline the Banja Luka organisation, and after that the organisation came under the direct control of the top leadership in Pale; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Karadzic often came to Banja Luka, and I believe that they did have these interparty discussions, but that is a bit different from what you said a moment ago, that there was subordination, so it's either one or the other. I don't know what they did at that meeting but it's only logical that the SDS of Banja Luka and the SDS of -- at republican level have co-ordination and co-operation and hierarchy, and I don't see anything problematic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there may not be any problematic aspects from your point of view about co-operation and co-ordination, but as you noted and then seemed to dispute, I was asking you about a kind of hierarchical issue. And the reality, Mr. Dodik, is that the portion of what I said that you seemed to dispute was precisely what you testified to in the Brdjanin case, where you said, again as I mentioned before, in the context of a discussion that had began in connection with an interview of 27 -- that is a newspaper interview of 27 February 1992, you said: "Later on, Karadzic came to Banja Luka to discipline the Banja Luka organisation, and after that the organisation came under the direct control of the top leadership in Pale." And you were asked when that was, and you said: "I know it was around those days and months, maybe May 1992." That's at 20544. So those were your words [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Okay. What's the problem? Did I say that I did not read that about Brdjanin? What I said then you really don't have to make the effort. Again, I'm prepared to sign everything that was said in the Brdjanin case, so I'm not denying that. I did not assume at all that you would be using that as the basic document in this examination because I expected us to talk about what I knew about Mr. Karadzic's work. However, in order to resolve the matter, and your efforts to prove my inconsistency, I am telling you that the stenographic notes of my Brdjanin testimony is something that I fully confirm but don't expect me to remember each and every word that I uttered seven or eight years ago. I really don't see anything problematic in that. I have no problem with that. What I said before the Trial Chamber in the Brdjanin case, I stand by that. I really cannot remember every sentence, every event. Don't expect me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not trying to -- it's not a memory quiz, Mr. Dodik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it would be of any assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it would be of any assistance we would agree that his entire transcript of his testimony in the Brdjanin case can be admitted in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, it's not a memory quiz. I'm not trying to catch you in what you can remember or not, but as you mentioned you wanted to talk about Mr. Karadzic's work and you talked about some aspects of what you consider to be his work. I'm talking about other aspects of his work, which I'm entitled to do. Again, it's also the case that the ARK assembly regulated all segments of life, and decisions were passed and observed by the municipalities that were members of the group; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Is that what the record of my testimony in the Brdjanin case says?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Then -- well, it's correct. No, no, no. It's all right. I agree with everything that was said in that case. You can read out the entire transcript. I'll just keep crying out yes. It's not a problem. So whatever was said there I stand by it. Every single word. And I'm not at a quiz. I know that perfectly well. I have come here to do a serious job as a responsible man, to talk about what I know about this, and I'm trying to be consistent in that and not to create confusion. So we have a very simple situation. What I said in the Brdjanin case is something that I stand by. You don't have to prove anything. Everything that the transcript records is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. But it's helpful -- thank you for that and I appreciate that but the Trial Chamber will expect me to identify particular aspects of that at appropriate times. So I wanted to move now to ask you about more specifically about something that was mentioned earlier, and that is that the SDS had their people posted in the media and in the police, among other structures, and I wanted to ask you about a particular aspect of the police, but in order to do that, I think it's necessary to move into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say so that it's correct, I requested that in the Brdjanin case, the private session, but not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank -- thank you for that clear indication, Mr. Dodik. So with respect to the issue of people posted in the police, it's correct then that the following is true, that the fame and notoriety of Ljuban's group was very strong everywhere in Banja Luka and everyone lived in fear of that group. Now, that was -- they became part of the police, right, as a special unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I mean, he -- it wasn't a special group and then became the police. He was the police from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he, that is Ecim, was on the one hand Karadzic's protege in Banja Luka; and on the other hand, he was very close to Arkan and his people. He, meaning Ecim, managed to create the impression that he was Karadzic's person there and that he was untouchable. And that's all correct; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: He has said, well, that he managed to create this impression. Now, whether it was so, it's something to be determined. The events indicate that he did have certain contacts with Arkan and that's also a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In -- what I just quoted -- what I just stated was, in fact, a quote from your testimony in Brdjanin as we've discussed before, and then you further elaborated on that saying: "Karadzic, Krajisnik, Stanisic, Mandic, Zupljanin and Ecim were part of one small compact team, and they were the most powerful people on their respective levels at the time." And that was correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course that they were the most powerful people; each one of them in his respective level of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They were part of one small, compact team. You stated that under oath also in Brdjanin; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, if that's what it says there, then I did state that of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I noted earlier, before asking you about the people that the SDS had posted in the police, which we just discussed to some extent, that you had also confirmed that they had their people posted in the media and I wanted to ask you some quick questions about that. First of all, the -- there was censorship of the media and control of the media, that is there was control up to the level of censorship, by the Ministry of Information, that is Mr. Ostojic, so that only what was suited to the authorities was published; right? And I think you were pretty clear about your position on propaganda in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, if that's recorded in the transcript, I stand by that, too. But now I can understand it from this point in time that it's quite logical that during wartime people act in this way. That was how the Croats acted, too, not just in Bosnia but in Croatia as well. That was how the Bosniaks acted as well. They had an influence on their media. It was also a sort of propaganda. That was what Milosevic was doing, everyone was. Slovenia was doing that, too, when it was preparing its secession from Yugoslavia led by Jelko Kacin, who is now an MP in the European parliament. He was the chief of the propaganda bureau for the violent secession, and today he's a European parliamentarian. So today I understand that this is something quite normal, that in time when you have such authorities and such things are happening, then information is shaped in a specific way, and everyone was doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And more specifically, in the area where you were, that is in the Krajina area or the Banja Luka area, there was the newspaper "Glas" and it -- "Glas" was only used for -- as propaganda, that is for propaganda purposes of the Serbian Democratic Party; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It could be found that about that paper. Is that recorded in the transcript that that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is recorded at 65 ter 24921 --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: All right, all right. If it's recorded then it's fine. It's all right. You don't have to ask me. Everything is fine. So if that's what is recorded there, everything is all right, and you don't have to ask me any questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please receive complete information about whether he said that in his testimony or if it's from his interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, this is the transcript from the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Dodik, that was the tape recorded transcript which has been transcribed; that is your words in B/C/S were transcribed into B/C/S again. You can see them if you want, but it is -- it's not something that someone thought they heard, it's a tape recorded interview. I wanted to ask you quickly about a particular --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: If you're trying to combine one and the other, I can understand that is your job, but what I'm trying to say here is that what I said in front of this respected Court before is something that I stand by, and also what I talked about with you in various situations is something that I never authorised. I never signed such a statement, and in that respect I cannot accept that this should be a basis for a claim for or against something. And thanks to Mr. Karadzic for his interventions, I have the impression that through these questions you're trying to relay only on what I said in the Brdjanin case. Once again in front of this Honourable Court I want to say that whatever I said in the Brdjanin case and whatever has been recorded here is something that I stand by, and with respect to that, I see no problem at all. Except that I apologise, I did not manage to remember every single detail. But once again I repeat, if that's what is recorded I'll stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll be more than happy to bring your attention to the distinction between the two. I understand your position now that simply because you said it can't be necessarily trusted, and then I'll bring to your attention what you stated verbatim and then you can tell us whether you stand by that or not. So is it the case that very often, that the SDS -- is it the case that the SDS presented itself as the protecter of the Serbian people, said that the Serbian people had to be protected from the Ustasha and other massacres, would go back to stories from World War II, but factually and in essence the idea was to gain power and to gain control over the whole area and to rule through the social institutions? Accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Legitimate political struggle, which implies of course legitimate means, assessments of events at the time among the Serbian people, there was tremendous fear from the rehabilitation of the Ustasha traditions because the memories of the Second World War were still quite fresh in the Krajina region. The Serbs had perished in great numbers in the Ustasha camp, Jasenovac, and the fear was more articulated through the people's conviction that it was possible that the crime against the Serbs would be repeated. And the Serbian Democratic Party, as a political party, believed that this fear was relevant, and of course it responded to it. So nothing is incorrect, nothing is anti-democratic about it if political option is trying to represent itself as the protecter of the people's national interests. This is what I'm doing in political practice in my political work nowadays. It is just that the frameworks are different or the moment is different with regard to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that was said at P -- in P24921, at pages 13 of the -- excuse me, at pages 3 of both the English and B/C/S but I wanted to move on very quickly to a specific example of the creation of a special atmosphere. Do you remember the arrival of the SOS in the Banja Luka area in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course I do. I talked about that as the then member of the police, at the Banja Luka airstrip. I was aware that they had arrived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a back drop to the questions I want to ask you, let's see if we can agree on that, that they came in as an armed group, they blocked the town, that they made certain demands, that a Crisis Staff was formed and acquiesced immediately to their demands; is that all correct so far?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: If I said it was so in the Brdjanin case, then it's fine. Now I do not remember any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the most detailed information on that is available in your tape-recorded interview so I'm not going to suggest that this was -- that I'm relying, in particular, on your Brdjanin testimony, but that's why I asked you about these very broad facts about the arrival and activities of the SOS. You can confirm that much, can't you, that they were armed, they blocked the town, they demanded -- made demands including -- made certain demands, that a Crisis Staff was formed consisting of highly placed Bosnian Serb officials, and they acquiesced virtually immediately to those demands?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It was quite a long time ago. It's possible that it was like that but I really cannot assert that now because quite a lot of time has passed since, and I cannot confirm any of the details any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we have more time I could put the specific quotes in front of you as a backdrop to what I'm going to ask you, but we can, keeping with our own practice, have those admitted to the Court. But you also noted in 2003 that these demands by this armed group, the SOS, were "practically the same as the SDS policy"; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I said that much time has elapsed. I would have to be reminded of all facts and then speak about it. It was long ago. I cannot confirm. But I repeat: If it was said in the Brdjanin case then I stand by it, but I can't confirm it off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, does this refresh your recollection any further? You also said that it was all planned and done within the SDS, through their people in the media, in the police, in the local administration, and when they, meaning the SOS, showed up, it was something they had already known, they would show, already knew they would show up. That's what you said in 2003, at pages 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The ruling political party, and it was the SDS at the time, of course affected social processes, and it's normal. The country was at war. And during that war those who got the confidence of the people certainly bore the greatest responsibility, and the SDS got the trust of the people. The people to a great extent stood by the SDS's programme. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I'm sorry, sir, I'm not talking about the people's reaction to this. I'm -- I -- I asked you specifically about whether the arrival of the SOS was something planned and done within the SDS, so if you don't remember that, we'll --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't remember. I cannot confirm it was a direct instruction of the SDS, but that group was there. That's beyond doubt. However, I was not involved in the decision-making bodies of the SDS. I don't know. I can tell you as what my reasoning is and my political analysis, but I'm their political opponent and was at the time too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, from your perspective as someone politically involved in both the republic level assembly and in events in Banja Luka, you also noted that with respect to the arrival of the SDS and these events that we've been discussing, that it happened because at that time: "The SDS was still trying to present its policies as something that could be accepted by the international factors, whereas, on the other hand, along some other lines it prepared all this." So that's what you stated before, that this was a particular technique used to move along different lines on the ground while saying something to the international community; correct? Saying something else to the international community.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I'm confused by your question. I can positively state that I wasn't present during these events and I didn't see President Karadzic, but the SDS was in power and executed its -- these powers on the ground and they were the political force that took the most far-reaching decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I see the time. If it is convenient, shall we take break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After the break can I expect that you could conclude in half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll absolutely do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll break for 40 minutes and resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, before we adjourned for the lunch recess, we had been discussing the events following the arrival of the SOS in Banja Luka, and the nature of those events and who was responsible, and I had asked you about the -- your comments from 2003 about the SDS trying to present its policies as something that could be accepted by the international factors, whereas, on the other hand, preparing things like this on the ground. Now, you also spoke in that context --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I cannot hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Our usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear it. But I didn't hear it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you hear me well in your language? Thank you. Please repeat, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was recapping what we had been discussing about the SOS and the SDS efforts to present its policies for the international factor on the one hand and to prepare events like this on the other, and in that context, you spoke about a specially created atmosphere. So I wanted to ask you briefly about that. What you said in 2003 was this was a specially created atmosphere and it was very easy to implement these things in such an atmosphere, and then you went on to talk about some of the things that were easy to implement in that atmosphere, including the dismissal of non-Serbs. Is that correct, that the atmosphere that was created at that time, as we previously discussed, made it easy to implement the dismissal of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course there was dismissal of non-Serbs, but Serbs were also dismissed in the territories controlled by the Muslims. That was part of the atmosphere created in the entire region, and it was war. I understand the role of Mr. Karadzic, who bears political responsibility for some events. But he stands accused for a joint criminal enterprise, which to my mind is a made-up category. And the things you've mentioned, well, everybody knows that people were dismissed to a greater or a lesser extent on all sides. I could testify about the political conditions in connection with the war in Bosnia, and how the war unfolded. It is very clear that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a unilateral secession and the international --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to -- I indicated I didn't want to interrupt but this is straying quite far from my question and back to the areas you were able to elucidate on at length in the examination-in-chief. Now, this is -- again you referred to the criminal enterprise, and I think you referred to that -- here you say it's a made-up category, earlier I think you said it was a manipulation. But, Mr. Dodik, that's not exactly what you were saying back around 2001, and when you --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: But such is life. We come to understand some things that may not have been clear to us. And now, if I may speak freely here, all these proceedings are based on the assumption that the Serbs were a factor of disorder and that everybody else was right. And that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, hold on just a second for a couple of reasons. Number 1, I will tell you that's frankly wrong and it's not the position of this institution or the Prosecution. And that -- or the Tribunal. But more importantly, for this -- at this moment, it's not at all what I'm asking you about. We are talking about what you said in 2001. You said, "That's possible." And among the things you stated back then, and I'll be happy to show you the newspaper articles in which those comments are reflected, was that you accused the SDS leadership of organising and committing crimes during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let's turn to P24906. Sorry, 65 ter 24906. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Excuse me, what did you say? Who did I state this to, some media?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to put this on the screen now. I think you said it to the regional parliament in Banja Luka but this is the media capturing some of those remarks. So this is a report from the BBC, the source of which is Beta news agency from Belgrade, from the 12th of January, 2001, noting that you accused the Serb Democratic Party of organising and committing crimes during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, saying it must be openly said that the crimes have been committed in this region under the SDS leadership and this must be punished, and noting the expectation that all leading SDS officials at various levels stand before The Hague Tribunal. That's --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Where does it say The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's in the second paragraph, sir. I think someone has got the cursor there now.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. That was the political struggle between me and the SDS in 2001. It was a time of transition of power. You can consider this as political discourse which need not necessarily be based on facts, but I'm not denying having said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6278, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I just mention, Mr. President, that the witness doesn't really read or speak English. So when we have only the English translation, it would be good if we went slowly so that he could actually understand the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I noted also that at the time, you were criticised by Mr. Kalinic for making those remarks, and in the course of that same article in which that's made, Mr. Kalinic spoke about the dire economic situation in the Bosnian Serb Republic with unemployment at the level of 40 per cent and many unemployed war veterans, and so on. That was an accurate assessment of Republika Srpska's economic situation post-war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: We are speaking about 2001. Nowadays it's difficult in Greece and Cyprus, too. Of course, the economic situation after a war is always a challenge. This only confirms what I have said just now. Mr. Kalinic was an SDS member. It is possible that I said this. I'm -- I don't remember everything, but I believe that it has been relayed accurately. By the way, I have so far given 20.000 interviews so I couldn't possibly remember each and every one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood. The reason I raise that is because you also alleged, not in 2001 but later, in both -- in 2005 and I believe afterwards, your concerns about and the fact that Mr. Karadzic had taken 36 million German marks from Banja Luka in the spring of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 24901. And that's available in the B/C/S as well so the witness can see it. That --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does B/C/S mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's an acronym we use here for the language Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian, so it all -- the witnesses of all ethnicities can understand the language spoken here.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: In -- where does it say in the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina that there is a Bosnian language? Okay. Never mind. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is no consensus about the Bosnian language. There is Serbian, there is Croatian, there is Bosniak, but no Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, you will see in whatever language you choose to characterise it in the left top column, the portion of the article that I wanted to draw your attention to, that there are documents about Radovan Karadzic taking 36 million German marks out of Banja Luka in a bag in spring 1997. First he took bills in the equivalent of 28 million German marks and then another 8 million on another occasion. And you were bringing this conduct by Mr. Karadzic to the attention of your community because you considered it unacceptable, incomprehensible, illegal, and, I presume, deeply unfair to the impoverished war veterans and widows.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. So what is your question? You want me to confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, but when I made this statement, I didn't know that this money was used for materiel for the reconstruction of the RS, especially the eastern part. It was used as deposit for roof tiles, bricks, and so on. But when I gave this statement, I didn't know it had been deposited in such a way. Under the conditions when there was -- when the payment system didn't work and all transactions were made in cash. Of course this is a huge amount. But later, when I became prime minister, I was able to see that merchandise worth more than 100 million marks had arrived, mostly for the reconstruction of the eastern part of Republika Srpska, above all the eastern part of Sarajevo. There is nothing contentious about this statement except for the fact that you're using the newspaper "Dnevni Avaz" which is a paper that we don't trust. We think that they are liars. I didn't deny what the BBC says, but the Bosniak newspaper "Dnevni Avaz" has been used for propaganda. It was a case then and it's still the case today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you confirm that particular article.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is this relevant, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This goes in -- both to the information that the witness had available about Dr. Karadzic generally before he came and attested to various aspects of his conduct and character, and it also relates to the reasons why he said he made the allegations in the previous article. And it will be tied in with another point I want to make as a general -- the general picture of the information available to this witness about the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The timing in which Mr. Karadzic allegedly took this money was 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we actually also think this is relevant because it shows that the witness learned things later after making some statements that turned out to be different than they were at the time. This is a good example of that. So we would also urge it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dodik, in the previous exhibit, that is 6278, there was reference in your -- in the comments that you made about the crimes that had been committed, also to your position that Mrs. Plavsic was ignored by the leading members of the party. And that, in part, that reflects your - I think what is no secret -- your close relationship with Mrs. Plavsic and your support of her over the years; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course, Mrs. Plavsic is a good and honourable woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were both aware of -- in contact with her and aware of her position in the Bosnian Serb leadership, relations with the members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, both during the war, in the immediate post-Dayton period, and even thereafter; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No. It's not so. Because I really came to know Ms. Plavsic and to associate with her only after 1998 or from mid-1997 onwards. She was the president and she was a prominent member of the SDS up until 1997 when the leadership parted ways and she slated elections as the president of the republic. After elections the government was supposed to be formed, and I accepted to take on this mandate for forming the government in 1997, and then I associated with her. I spent a lot of time with her, and this is why I can say that she is a really good and honourable woman and a great patriot, and so on. As for the events before that time, that is to say before the war, during the war and after the war, I knew Ms. Plavsic, I heard about her, I met her sometimes during the assembly sessions, but we didn't have a close relation. And as for the claims that you expressed, I can only say that that was an opinion but that was not even confirmed within the SDS, such relations between us at an earlier time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough about your relations. But you spoke with her subsequently, as I believe you indicated, you testified for her during the course of her sentencing hearing here about, among other things, the difficulties she had with other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. And that was why they parted ways. I just said that in mid-1997, when Karadzic was no longer actively involved in politics, there was a rift in the leadership of the SDS and Ms. Plavsic continued to perform her office, and if things were not so dramatic there would not have been a rift. And they parted ways because they had parted ways politically about certain issues, and that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you became aware specifically, did you not, of her continuing conflict with Momcilo Mandic, among others?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. That conflict was generally known throughout the time while it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And specifically what Mrs. Plavsic has made no secret about whatsoever, and I therefore presume that you had opportunities to discuss it with her, was the onset of that conflict which began in 1992, as she related in her book, "I testify" when she brought to the attention of the Bosnian Serb leadership the activities of Batko in Grbavica. And she described in detail how she went to a meeting involving Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic, told them what she had learned about Batko, was stunned that Mandic simply smirked about it and that she realised that both Mandic and Stanisic knew about him and his activities and indeed were his protecters and order-givers, and then explained since then - and believed it would surely be like to the end of her life - Mandic had been harassing and threatening her. You were aware of all that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Years later, I learned the actual substance you're talking about but I did not attend the meeting that you mentioned and I cannot confirm that I know that. I did hear that a meeting was held. I'm not sure whether this one, Batko, was mentioned then or not. But I do know, and one could feel when we attended the assembly session, it was known among the MPs that the relations between Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Mandic were not at the level that was expected between members of the Presidency of Republika Srpska and the minister in the Republika Srpska government. So this was felt and known. And later on, Ms. Plavsic herself told me about some of these things, this meeting and some problems that she had, but this is more or less everything I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- give me just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You spoke earlier today about Mr. Sejmenovic, and the story you described as I see it here now --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You remember Mr. Sejmenovic? Because you testified about him earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's the man with that last name but it's easy to check. He was in the assembly and I met him in Banja Luka under circumstances I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the circumstances you describe to this Trial Chamber today was that in the early part of May, around the 10th or 12th of May, you went to see Mr. Sejmenovic where he was living, went over to his house, to have a discussion with him. He was concerned about or had some fear about possible developments so you invited him to work with the assembly or in the assembly of Republika Srpska, thought he had accepted but he later declined and that this was the -- you related that to him, that this was something that Mr. Karadzic had approved. Mr. Dodik, the fact is that this was not a benevolent invitation to suggest to somebody that he might want to consider joining the Bosnian Serb assembly under conditions where he could freely choose whether or not to do so. The fact is that this man -- this was not early May. But this man had just been taken out of Omarska; correct? And that's what you testified to in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Several things. Yes, he did come from Omarska. He arrived in Banja Luka. We talked. I was not myself free. Under such uncertain conditions, nobody was free. We discussed, we believed that by his engagement he could eliminate the fear that existed in a significant degree and that was the subject of our discussion. I didn't say earlier that Mr. Karadzic accepted this in advance, but we said that we discussed that later. Mr. Karadzic didn't even know that we were discussing about this. I believe that for reasons that we were colleagues, I should talk with him, and I did it not just alone but with Vojo Kupresanin, who was also an SDS MP in the assembly at the time. So we talked about the issue and I don't see anything wrong there. These were the first months -- he had no more or less freedom than I had to decide what and how to do at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This man was scared to death; right? He was very frightened and he bore the physical effects of his time in Omarska. You could see it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see any consequences. One could see a degree of exhaustion. I was very surprised. I do not scare anyone to death. And when I was there, I did not notice that he was scared to death of that conversation. After that, as far as I could follow, nothing happened to that man later. I couldn't follow everything, though, but in the first few weeks after that event, I think that he did not have any problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Just so we don't get caught up in semantics, let's set aside "scared to death" and whatever that means to you. Are you saying you couldn't tell this man was very frightened?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, I just said that I saw that there was some fear, but I did not see any physical marks of violence. I didn't see. Perhaps that was under his clothes, but I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I think I'm at my half hour, Mr. President, and that concludes the examination, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very few questions, Your Honours, very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, something that you stated was quoted to you as recorded in "Dnevni Avaz." Were your statements given as part of your political struggle conveyed precisely in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course not always, depending on the leanings of each medium, it depended on that because they are not really responsible in terms of the media freedom, as we can see in the west. This is why their articles do not always stick to the facts. And most often this is the case with, for example, "Dnevni Avaz" which is a well known paper of the Bosniak people which was formed during the war and performed its propaganda role practically throughout this time. And even to this day, in some of its elements, as well as "Glasovski [phoen]" which was active in our part of Bosnia and about which Mr. Prosecutor also asked me it preferred such contents that was in accordance not just with the official policy but the general atmosphere of the specific moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pause. Pause, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat such statements under oath, such as you accepted everything that you had said under oath in the Brdjanin case? Would you likewise repeat everything that was said in the media under oath?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Certainly not. Not under oath. But as for this specific issue, I think that I explained everything that I said, and I did say that under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we just briefly see P6278, just to clarify something semantically. This is your statement given to the BBC. And could we please zoom in a bit? Mr. President, I'm going to read this out slowly in the English language so that it would be interpreted: [In English] "It must be openly said that crimes have been committed in this region under the SDS leadership." [Interpretation] Was it the region that was under the SDS leadership or did SDS lead in the crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No. The SDS did not lead in this. The SDS was the leading political party and that was the context in which this was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am accused here not because a party was formed and structured and was successful in elections. Rather, I'm accused for being involved in the commission of crimes. From what you know, what can you say about my possible involvement in crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: With full responsibility and under oath, I can say here that I never had the occasion at any meeting or when I met personally with Mr. Karadzic, most often during assembly sessions that were held during the war, I never heard the request being made to anyone to commit any crime. Rather, I can repeat that Mr. Karadzic resolutely tried to find a way to resolve the conflicts peacefully and that the responsibility for crimes which were committed by certain paramilitaries in the territory of Republika Srpska, that they needed to be taken to responsibility for that. Of course it was a situation that is not normal. It was war. And as I say here, I absolutely assert that Mr. Karadzic never insisted on the commission of any crimes, nor did I witness that he was involved in anything like that. What I believe needs to be said are the circumstances under which that happened. At the very beginning of the war, I did say something about that previously. But the key issue remains, and these are the relations among the ethnicities, Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have the consensus for unilateral secession. Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have to object. This is -- the witness is straying into further elucidation of a favourite theme that is not related to the question asked, calls for an objection as being non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered the question already. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will return to something you did not finish. I would like to ask you the following: Were you a member of the War Presidency in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. Laktasi municipality. As a deputy, I was supposed to be involved in this. The SDS had the majority in this municipality. That is to say that the municipal officials came from the SDS. And I was also a member of this War Presidency as a member of another political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were that officially, by nature of your position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, by the nature of my position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ex officio, yes, fine. In the Presidency did you receive any orders from the Crisis Staff of the ARK, which you then had to implement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't remember such a situation at all. We regularly corresponded with them, but I don't remember any specific orders about anything, so I cannot confirm that that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Chamber whether the Crisis Staffs, the Presidencies, and some other ad hoc bodies in which people held their positions ex officio were unlawful or illegal according to our laws?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: In all extraordinary situations and war is certainly an extraordinary situation, this was considered something normal, and when there are major floodings in the municipal area, then a Crisis Staff is normally set up. Under the conditions that I talked about, that is to say the isolation and social depravity, it was to be expected that such a body would be formed. I also wish to say that throughout the time while I was a member of the War Presidency of the Laktasi municipality, the Municipal Assembly was also operational, and the War Presidency at least in that municipality did not substitute the work of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President I will read out to you, and this is P6, a Prosecution document, it says, pursuant to Article 12 of the Law on All People's Defence, and the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, the Executive Council of the Autonomous Region of Krajina at its meeting of the 5th of May, 1992, adopted the following decision to form the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. So here they refer to Article 12 of the Law on National Defence. From what you know about municipalities, what role did the president of the municipality, or the president of any socio-political community have in the national defence of his own area, if he had any such role?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Up until the first multi-party elections held in 1990, I had been a municipal official. I was in charge of the executive power in Laktasi municipality, and together with the municipal president I undoubtedly had the obligation to follow all plans and to introduce innovations with regard to the security situation in the territory of the municipality that I belonged to. With regard to this, the president of the municipality was the leader in charge of all the war plans which according to the law at the time all municipalities had to have, so he was in charge. He managed those plans as the president of the municipality and in accordance with the Law on All People's Defence of the former Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please speak much slower, please. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, you were asked about the structure of parties and so on. Please tell us if, in your party, decisions are taken in a democratic fashion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course they are. The respective body sits, there is discussion about the matter in question, a common position is articulated, and then the executive bodies or me as the president, are then called upon to execute this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In my party or any party, who has the power to change a democratically taken decision in the -- at the implementation stage?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: If given explicit powers in line with the statute the party president can do so, but he must consult the party bodies to get approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if during the implementation stage you demand discipline and in the implementation of democratically taken decisions, would you call that autocratic ruling?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No, that's a democratic system of responsibility, with which all party members must abide by. Whoever does not is infringing upon party discipline and must bear the consequences in line with the party standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under conditions where everybody can found a party, would it be allowed and honourable to implement the programme of one party in another party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course not. There is absolute liberty where we are from, and we are one of the few countries where there is a huge number of political parties. If they disagree with the articulated policy of one party, they -- people are free to found their own, and I don't see why I would carry out anybody's instructions if I'm a member of a different party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today on page 44, it is recorded that you said that I was the uncontested leader of the SDS. Was this leadership achieved by undemocratic means, or did I have any means of coercion before the war or during the war to force the members of the SDS to have me as their uncontested leader?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: You certainly are an uncontested leader. The people saw you as such. And by virtue of that your statements and your conduct had the support of the whole people. As far as I know, and that can be confirmed by any serious assessment, the SDS was a movement that included everybody who wanted to join it and be members of that political party. I cannot confirm because I don't know. I was not witness to any instance of undemocratic membership or your exerting coercion against any member of your party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 43, it was quoted to you what the Serbian forces were doing. Can you, as a high official of the assembly now also of the republic and previously of the executive power at municipal level, say which armed group or individuals you would consider Serbian forces, for which the authorities are responsible and were there any whom you would not consider Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Only the army of the police of the Republika Srpska are legitimate structures, and there were groups who -- which at the local level abusing the impossibility to communicate, and also by using elements of violence, there were some paramilitary groups that were not under the control of the authorities and even exercised repression against local authorities of the RS at certain periods. And these paramilitary or militant organisations and individuals absolutely were not under the influence of the local structures of power in the RS. I can say, having been in contact with General Talic, who was a commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, that he made efforts to place -- or, even to place under control or even disarm these paramilitary formations in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you spoke about the protection of the Muslim community at Laktasi during the examination-in-chief, let me now repeat the question because I didn't receive a complete answer. What was the source of jeopardy for these Muslims? Was it the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No. They wanted to be protected by the authorities, and they got that protection. I was a representative of the authorities and I've already said that as commander of a military police unit at Banja Luka airstrip I stood up for them and they were threatened by undefined groups that weren't even made up of locals. They would suddenly turn up somewhere, suddenly appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for the efforts you made to come here and testify.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I have leave just to clarify one tiny characterisation that Mr. Karadzic made that was contrary to what I said? Maybe the witness needs to confirm. It's with respect to P62, I think it's 78, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, very quickly, with respect to that BBC article that captured your remarks about the SDS and leadership and crimes committed in the region that Mr. Karadzic asked you about, that was not a statement given directly to the BBC, was it? That was a statement to the regional assembly in Banja Luka that the BBC picked up; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: You said it was Beta and then the BBC. I cannot tell which it was, but the only reliable source is the minutes of the assembly, but I believe I was able to clarify the SDS at the time was the undisputed ruler in the area. But I didn't see SDS units or I didn't see political commissioners in the military units that ran the operations. There was no such thing. And as for the responsibility of the authorities, of course authorities are responsible anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. President Dodik, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness is not available until tomorrow morning, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why is it so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's because I estimated that Mr. Dodik would take the entire day and I've been asked by the victim and witnesses section not to keep witnesses waiting too long, so I tried to balance those two considerations, and as a result I told him he could just be ready for 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Being late this morning was also contributing to sending witness back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 at Courtroom III. I was informed that everything is now okay in there. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of April, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.38 p.m.,
